1023.title: The resolve that opens a puja
1023.hook: before a puja, the priest names the age of the world and the family's name, then begins
1023.carry: sankalpa: my small act, placed in God's time
1023.howItsDone: Before a puja or a vrata, the priest or householder makes a sankalpa, often holding water in the right hand, naming the age of the world, the place, the date, the person and family line, and the purpose; guided yoga nidra opens and closes with a short sankalpa of the practitioner's own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra with Patanjali: too much sleep is tamas, not yoga.

Sunday morning at a grandmother's house, smelling of ghee and marigolds. A priest sits cross-legged before a small altar, and before a single flower is offered, he asks a question. Your name? Your gotra, your family line? Then he takes a little water in his right hand and starts reciting, quickly, in Sanskrit: a long string about the second half of Brahma's life, the age of the White Boar, the Kali Yuga, this land, this day. Only then does the puja begin.
screen: `GHEE AND MARIGOLDS.` → `YOUR NAME? YOUR GOTRA?` → `THE AGE OF THE WORLD, THEN TODAY'S DATE.`

segments.voice: That recitation is the sankalpa, the resolve, and in a common form it begins with the whole of time. The second half of Brahma's life. The kalpa, the cosmic day, called Shveta Varaha, the White Boar. That name carries a story. The Bhagavata Purana tells that the earth once sank deep into the cosmic waters, and Brahma, just beginning to make the world, didn't know how to bring her back. Then from his nostril came a tiny boar, no bigger than a thumb. It grew, and grew, until it filled the sky. It was Vishnu. He dove into the flood, found the earth at the bottom, and lifted her up on his tusks while the sages sang his praise. Our cosmic day carries the name of that rescue. Then it zooms in: this age, the Kali Yuga; this land; this year, month and day; this person, this family line; and this purpose. Here's the teaching: in Hindu worship, an offering isn't tossed off. Before you act, you say who you are, where you stand in God's vast time, and why you're doing it. Then you offer it. A single flower becomes a deliberate act, set inside a story as old as the earth's rescue. That's why the word turned up in the mantra days, and why yoga nidra borrowed it. Swami Satyananda of the Bihar School, who set out the guided form, opens and closes the practice with a sankalpa: short, sincere, at the start and again near the end. Rest, like worship, begins on purpose.
screen: `SANKALPA: THE RESOLVE THAT OPENS A PUJA.` · `OUR COSMIC DAY: THE WHITE BOAR.` · `VISHNU LIFTS THE EARTH ON HIS TUSKS.` · `THE AGE, THE PLACE, THE DAY, THE PERSON, THE PURPOSE.` · then, large: `MY SMALL ACT, PLACED IN GOD'S TIME.`

segments.voice: Sit up for a moment. If you pray, cup a little water in your right hand, or simply cup the hand, and make a tiny sankalpa in your own words: who you are, today's date, where you are, and what you offer this rest for; then let the water go, or open the hand. If you don't pray, say it as a quiet promise. Now lie back, hear the far sounds, the near ones, the breath, and rest. Near the end, say your sankalpa once more.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, which in its guided form opens and closes with a sankalpa, the same resolve that opens a puja.
Your line: sankalpa, my small act, placed in God's time. The White Boar's day, and yours. Until tomorrow.

1024.title: The rays gather into the sun
1024.hook: at sunset the sun's rays gather back into the sun, and an Upanishad says the senses do the same at night
1024.carry: pratyahara: the senses drawn back in
1024.howItsDone: In guided yoga nidra, the teacher names parts of the body in a set order and listeners place attention on each without moving; teachers describe this rotation of awareness as a doorway to pratyahara, the withdrawal of the senses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sankalpa: my small act, placed in God's time, at the start of a puja and of yoga nidra.
screen: `SANKALPA.` · `MY SMALL ACT, PLACED IN GOD'S TIME.`

segments.voice: Six seekers walk to a sage's hermitage with firewood in their hands, the old sign of students asking to be taught. The sage, Pippalada, tells them: live here a year first, then ask. A year later, one of them, Gargya, asks about the body at night. When a person sleeps, what is it in them that sleeps? And what stays awake? Pippalada answers with the evening sky. At sunset, he says, the rays of the sun all gather back into that one disc of light. At sunrise they spread out again. That's what happens to the senses every night.
screen: `FIREWOOD IN HAND. A YEAR OF WAITING.` → `WHAT SLEEPS? WHAT STAYS AWAKE?` → `THE RAYS GATHER INTO THE SUN.`

segments.voice: That's the Prashna Upanishad, the Upanishad of Questions, and the fourth question is Gargya's. Pippalada's answer, in paraphrase: as the rays of the setting sun become one in its disc of light, so in sleep all the senses become one in the mind, the highest of them. Then the person doesn't hear, see, smell, taste or touch, speak, take hold or move. And people say, he sleeps. Yet the breaths keep watch in the city of the body, like fires kept burning in a house. Under the picture sits a teaching Hindu schools share: the senses are the mind's instruments, sent out by day, not the self that sends them. Sleep gathers them in without asking. Patanjali has a name for gathering them in on purpose, while awake. In the second chapter of the Yoga Sutras he calls it pratyahara: the senses withdrawing from their objects and following the mind inward. The Gita gives the picture: a tortoise drawing in its limbs. Satyananda describes yoga nidra as a way into pratyahara, and the main tool is a quick tour of the body called the rotation of awareness. The guide names a part, the right-hand thumb, the palm, the wrist, and the listener places attention there, without moving. It looks like doing very little. But it's the senses being gathered back into the mind, the way Pippalada saw the rays gathered into the sun, only this time on purpose.
screen: `THE SENSES BECOME ONE IN THE MIND.` · `THE BREATHS KEEP WATCH, LIKE FIRES.` · `THE SENSES ARE INSTRUMENTS, NOT THE SELF.` · `PRATYAHARA: THE SENSES DRAWN IN.` · then, large: `THE RAYS GATHER INTO THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Lie down or sit back with eyes closed, and without moving, let attention go where it's named: right-hand thumb, second finger, third, fourth, fifth, palm, back of the hand, wrist, elbow, shoulder, right side of the chest, right hip, knee, ankle, right big toe. Now the whole right side, all at once. Then let attention rest on the breath, keeping watch, like a fire kept burning in a house.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, where pratyahara gathers the senses into the mind, like rays into the setting sun, this time on purpose.
Your line: pratyahara, the senses drawn back in, like rays into the setting sun. Tomorrow, the one who stays awake. See you tomorrow.

1025.title: The witness who never sleeps
1025.hook: the Katha Upanishad speaks of one who stays awake in those who sleep
1025.carry: sakshi: the witness awake in those who sleep
1025.howItsDone: Hindus who study Vedanta speak of the sakshi, the witness that remains through waking, dream and deep sleep; teachers of yoga nidra describe the practice as deep rest for the body with awareness kept awake.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra and pratyahara: the senses drawn back in, as pratyahara: the senses drawn back in.

A night nurse walks a quiet ward at three in the morning. Every bed holds a sleeper. Some breathe slowly. One talks in a dream. One turns over and pulls the blanket up. The nurse is the only one awake, moving from bed to bed, seeing it all, waking no one. The Katha Upanishad has a line that sounds like that ward, but it's describing something inside each sleeper. It says someone stays awake in us while we sleep.
screen: `A QUIET WARD AT THREE A.M.` → `EVERY BED HOLDS A SLEEPER.` → `ONE IS AWAKE, WAKING NO ONE.`

segments.voice: The Katha Upanishad is Death's teaching to a boy named Nachiketas, who went to Death's house and waited three nights without food until Death came home and, as a host who had kept a guest waiting, owed him three wishes. His last wish was to know what lies beyond death. In the fifth section of Death's answer comes this, in paraphrase. The Person who is awake in those who sleep, shaping one desire after another, that is the bright one, that is Brahman, that alone is called the deathless. Even while we dream, something is awake and doing the shaping. Hindus call it the atman, the Self: not the body, not the thoughts, but the one who sees them. The Gita turns the image around. What is night for all beings, Krishna says in chapter two, in that the self-mastered one is awake. The world's busy daytime is a kind of sleep, and what the world sleeps through, the sage is awake to. Another Upanishad gives this watcher a name: sakshi, the witness. The Shvetashvatara calls the one God, hidden in all beings, the witness, the one who knows, alone, beyond the qualities. That's where the yoga nidra days have been heading: the Goddess holding Vishnu's sleep, the Mandukya's fourth, the resolve, the senses gathered in. Read side by side, each can be taken as pointing toward one thing: rest so deep it looks like sleep, with the witness still awake. Teachers of the practice say it plainly: the body sleeps, and awareness doesn't.
screen: `NACHIKETAS WAITS THREE NIGHTS AT DEATH'S DOOR.` · `AWAKE IN THOSE WHO SLEEP.` · `THE ATMAN: THE ONE WHO SEES.` · `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS.` · then, large: `THE BODY SLEEPS. AWARENESS DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: Lie down or sit back, eyes closed, and let the body go heavy, one part at a time, while the breath does what it does. Then notice that something is noticing all this: the heaviness, the breath, a sound in the room, a stray thought. Don't try to find the noticer or picture it; just rest as the one who sees, like the nurse on the ward, waking no one.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. Deep rest for the body, with the witness, the sakshi, still awake.
Your line: sakshi, the witness awake in those who sleep. Tomorrow, the eyes open, on a single flame. Sleep well tonight.

1026.title: Shiva's still gaze
1026.hook: the gods send desire to break Shiva's meditation, and one flame from his third eye ends it
1026.carry: trataka: the great yogi's still gaze
1026.howItsDone: Practitioners of hatha yoga do trataka by gazing steadily at a small point, often a candle flame or a shrine lamp at eye level, then closing the eyes to rest; many Hindus picture Shiva, the great yogi, seated with this kind of steady gaze. Teachers advise against gazing at the sun.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed yoga nidra with the sakshi, the witness awake in those who sleep. Today the eyes open.
screen: `YOGA NIDRA.` · `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS, AWAKE IN SLEEP.`

segments.voice: High in the Himalaya, Shiva sits in meditation, so still the forest around him goes quiet. The gods need him to wake. A demon named Taraka is crushing the worlds, and only a son of Shiva can stop him. So they send Kama, the god of desire, with a bow of sugarcane and arrows made of flowers. Spring arrives out of season. The young Parvati comes near with an offering of flowers. Kama draws the bow.
screen: `SHIVA, STILL ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `THE GODS SEND DESIRE.` → `KAMA DRAWS THE BOW.`

segments.voice: For a moment, the poet Kalidasa says, Shiva's calm stirs, like the ocean when the moon rises, and his eyes turn toward Parvati's face. Then he catches himself, looks around for what moved him, and sees Kama with the bow drawn. A flame leaps from the third eye in his forehead, and the god of desire falls as ash. Hindus know this story from the Shiva Purana and from Kalidasa's Birth of the War God, and it's one reason Shiva is called Mahayogi, the great yogi. In temple images and home pictures he sits with eyes half closed, gaze steady, untouched by every pull. Hatha yoga calls him Adinatha, the first teacher. In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, that tradition's best-known manual, trataka is one of six cleansing acts. In paraphrase: with a still mind, gaze with fixed eyes at a small mark until tears come. The text says it drives away tandra, the heavy dullness that settles on a mind. Notice what's being cleaned: not the skin, the attention. The eye spends the day darting from screen to face to sign, and trataka asks it to do one thing and stay. Many teachers read the Kama story the same way: a mind whose gaze is steady isn't dragged off by every arrow. That isn't a verdict that desire is evil; in the Puranas, Kama is born again. But the yogi chooses where to look. A word of care: never gaze at the sun, and blink when the eyes ask. The tears are a sign of the held gaze, not a goal.
screen: `A FLAME FROM THE THIRD EYE. KAMA FALLS AS ASH.` · `MAHAYOGI: SHIVA, THE GREAT YOGI.` · `TRATAKA: A STILL GAZE AT A SMALL MARK.` · `IT CLEANS THE ATTENTION.` · then, large: `THE YOGI CHOOSES WHERE TO LOOK.`

segments.voice: If you keep a shrine, sit before its lamp or a picture of Shiva; if not, choose one small point at eye level, a mark on the wall or a candle safely lit, never the sun. Look at it, not around it, letting the eyes soften and stay, and blink when you need to; this is not a contest. When the eyes tire, close them and rest, then open them and look again. If your eyes are sore or unwell, simply sit with them closed.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point, until the eyes water. In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, one of the six cleansing acts.
Your line: trataka, the great yogi's still gaze. Shiva's way: one small point, and the eyes stay. Until tomorrow.

1027.title: A lamp where no wind blows
1027.hook: a clay lamp on a windowsill lies flat when the door opens, and stands up again when it shuts
1027.carry: abhyasa and vairagya: practice, and letting go
1027.howItsDone: Some who practice trataka use a candle or ghee lamp set at eye level in a still, draft-free room, and some recall the Gita's image of a lamp in a windless place as they sit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka began: the great yogi's still gaze, Shiva's own, on one small mark.

A small clay lamp sits on a windowsill, a cotton wick in a pool of oil. Someone opens the front door. A draft runs through the house, and the flame lies down sideways, thin and blue, nearly out. The door shuts. For a moment the flame shivers. Then it stands back up, tall and still, as if nothing happened. A small drama, easy to miss. The Bhagavad Gita uses that same flame to describe a mind.
screen: `A CLAY LAMP ON A WINDOWSILL.` → `THE DOOR OPENS. THE FLAME LIES DOWN.` → `THE DOOR SHUTS. IT STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: In chapter six of the Gita, Krishna describes someone sitting in meditation, and then gives a single picture. In paraphrase: as a lamp in a place without wind does not flicker, so is the mind of the yogi who has gathered it in. Kalidasa, in yesterday's story, paints the meditating Shiva the same way: like a lamp unmoving where no wind blows. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say the yogi has no mind, or that the flame goes out. The lamp is still burning, still giving light. What's gone is the flicker. Arjuna, listening, isn't convinced. A few verses later he pushes back: the mind is restless, Krishna, stubborn and strong, and holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. It's an honest complaint, and the text keeps it in. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees the mind is hard to hold. Then he names two things that hold it: abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go. Practice is coming back, again and again. Letting go is not feeding every draft that blows through. Earlier in the same chapter, Krishna puts the coming back in plain terms: wherever the restless mind wanders off, draw it back from there, and rest it again in the Self. That's why the flame suits trataka so well. The eyes rest on the very thing the Gita compares the mind to. The practice is simply to notice when attention leans, like a flame in a draft, and come back. The Gita never promises the wind will stop forever. It describes a lamp in a sheltered place, and a person who keeps coming back to it.
screen: `A LAMP WHERE NO WIND BLOWS.` · `ARJUNA: AS HARD AS HOLDING THE WIND.` · `ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA: PRACTICE, AND LETTING GO.` · `WHEREVER IT WANDERS, DRAW IT BACK.` · then, large: `THE FLAME STILL BURNS. ONLY THE FLICKER GOES.`

segments.voice: Set a candle flame safely lit, or a mark on the wall, at eye level, and let the eyes rest on it, blinking whenever you need to. Each time a sound, a plan or a memory pulls you away, notice the lean, like a flame in a draft, and come back to the point: no scolding, just return. If the eyes tire, close them for a while, then open them and look again.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, with the Gita's lamp in a windless place, and the coming back each time the mind leans.
Your line: abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go. The flame still burns; only the flicker goes. See you tomorrow.

1028.title: Eyes turned around
1028.hook: a child stares at a light bulb, squeezes her eyes shut, and finds a glowing shape still floating there
1028.carry: turn the eyes around, toward the self within
1028.howItsDone: Some teachers of trataka pair the open-eyed gaze at a flame with a closed-eyed phase, in which the practitioner holds the after-image in attention until it fades, then gazes again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita's lamp in a windless place: abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go.

A child lies on her bed staring up at the light bulb, because someone told her not to. Then she squeezes her eyes shut. And there it is: a glowing shape floating in the dark behind her eyelids, green, then purple, drifting when she moves her eyes. She opens them, stares again, shuts them again, delighted. It's a game. In trataka, the same thing happens, and it isn't treated as a side effect. Some teachers make it the second half.
screen: `STARE AT THE LIGHT. SHUT THE EYES.` → `A GLOWING SHAPE STAYS.` → `NOT A SIDE EFFECT. THE SECOND HALF.`

segments.voice: Some teachers of trataka describe it in two parts. Outer trataka is the gaze on the flame or the mark, eyes open. Inner trataka begins when the eyes close: the image left behind is held in attention, gently, for as long as it lasts. When it fades, some teachers say to keep looking into the place where it was, or to open the eyes and gaze again. The practice moves the same object from in front of the eyes to behind them. Why bother? In the Katha Upanishad, Death, still teaching the boy Nachiketas, names the problem the second half answers. In paraphrase: the Self-existent one pierced the openings of the senses outward, so a person looks outward, and not at the Self within. But a certain wise one, wanting the deathless, turned the eyes around and saw the Self within. Eyes turned around: that's the heart of it. The senses are made to face out, sight especially, running ahead of us all day to the next screen, the next face, the next sign. The verse doesn't blame the eyes for that. It says that's how they were made. Then it describes someone who, for once, turns them back, toward the atman, the Self, the same witness that stays awake in sleep. Trataka does this in a very literal, very small way. The outer gaze gathers attention onto one point. Then the eyelids close, and that same gathered attention points inward at an image that exists only on the inside. It isn't the Upanishad's whole vision, only a training run: a minute of turning the eyes around.
screen: `OUTER TRATAKA: EYES OPEN, ON THE FLAME.` · `INNER TRATAKA: THE IMAGE BEHIND THE LIDS.` · `THE SENSES WERE MADE TO FACE OUT.` · `THE WISE ONE TURNED THE EYES AROUND, TOWARD THE SELF.` · then, large: `FROM THE FLAME OUT THERE TO THE FLAME IN HERE.`

segments.voice: Set a candle flame or a small, bright mark at eye level, never the sun, and gaze at it softly for a few breaths, blinking when you need to. Then close the eyes and hold the image it left behind without squinting or chasing it, noticing its color, where it drifts, how it fades. When it's gone, rest in the dark where it was for a breath or two, then open the eyes and gaze again.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, both halves: the flame in front of the eyes, and the image held behind them.
Your line: turn the eyes around, toward the Self within. The flame out there, the flame in here. Until tomorrow.

1029.title: Parvati holds her mind on Shiva
1029.hook: a stranger mocks the god Parvati has chosen, and her mind doesn't move
1029.carry: dharana: the mind held on one beloved form
1029.howItsDone: In yoga traditions that follow Patanjali, trataka is taught as a training in dharana, holding attention on a single chosen object; many Hindus choose an image of their ishta devata, their chosen form of God, while others use a flame, a mark or a flower.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eyes turned around, toward the Self within: outer trataka, then inner.

After Kama burned, Parvati didn't give up. If beauty couldn't reach Shiva, she would reach him another way. She left her father's palace for the mountains and began tapas, austerity, her whole mind set on Shiva. Summer heat, winter water, rain. In time she stopped eating even fallen leaves, and people called her Aparna, the one without a leaf. Then one day a young ascetic with matted hair walks into her hermitage, and starts to talk.
screen: `PARVATI LEAVES THE PALACE.` → `APARNA: NOT EVEN A LEAF.` → `A STRANGER WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: He's charming, and he's sure she's wasting herself. Shiva? the stranger says, in Kalidasa's telling. He haunts cremation grounds, wears snakes, rides an old bull, and nobody knows his birth. Parvati's answer is fierce: you don't know him, and I won't hear another word. She turns to leave. And the stranger catches her hand: it's Shiva himself. From today, he says, I'm yours, won by your tapas. Hindus tell this as the road to the wedding of Shiva and Parvati, and many teachers read it as a picture of a mind that has found its place and won't be pried away. Patanjali has a word for that. The third chapter of the Yoga Sutras opens with dharana, in paraphrase: the binding of the mind to a place. The word comes from the root dhri, to hold, the same root as dharma. The next sutra names what grows from it: dhyana, meditation, when attention flows to that place unbroken. And what should the place be? Vyasa's commentary names the navel, the tip of the nose, or an outer object, and in the first chapter Patanjali adds, in paraphrase: or by meditating on whatever one finds agreeable. That leaves room for what so many Hindus already do: hold the mind on their own chosen form of God, their ishta devata: Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess, Ganesha. Trataka is dharana you can see. The flame, the mark or the beloved image sits right there, and when the mind wanders, you walk it back. Parvati didn't hold on by force. She held on because she loved what she was holding.
screen: `THE STRANGER MOCKS SHIVA. PARVATI WON'T HEAR IT.` · `IT WAS SHIVA: 'I'M YOURS, WON BY YOUR TAPAS.'` · `DHARANA: THE MIND HELD TO ONE PLACE.` · `WHATEVER ONE FINDS AGREEABLE.` · then, large: `TRATAKA IS DHARANA YOU CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: Choose your place: if you pray, a picture of the form of God you love; if not, a candle safely lit, a mark on the wall or a flower. Set it at eye level and rest the eyes on it. When the mind wanders, notice it, and walk it back without scolding, the way Parvati turned back to Shiva season after season. If the eyes tire, close them and keep the form in mind.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, dharana you can see: the mind held on one place, or one beloved form.
Your line: dharana, the mind held on one beloved form. A week of resolve, gathering and gaze. Same time tomorrow.
